content_html:
An annuity has two phases. During accumulation you pay in, either a single premium or regular additions, and the balance grows at a credited rate. During payout the balance is turned into a stream of income. This calculator projects the accumulation phase year by year and then estimates the level monthly income the ending balance could support over a period you choose.

How to use this calculator

  1. Starting principal: the amount you put in at the outset, such as a single premium or a rollover.
  2. Yearly and monthly additions: regular amounts you add. You can use either or both; leave unused boxes at 0.
  3. Annual growth rate: the yearly rate credited to the balance after fees. For a fixed annuity this is the guaranteed or declared rate; for anything else it is an assumption.
  4. Years to grow: how long the accumulation phase lasts.
  5. Addition timing: at the start of each period (an annuity due) or at the end (an ordinary annuity).
  6. Income from the balance: how many years the payout lasts and the rate the remaining balance earns while it is paid out.

How the figures are calculated

The growth rate is treated as an effective yearly rate, so the balance grows by (1 + r)1/12 − 1 each month. That way monthly and yearly additions are handled consistently: a yearly addition earns exactly the stated rate over a full year. With additions at the end of each year only, the ending balance matches the textbook formula

Balance = P × (1 + r)n + A × [(1 + r)n − 1] ÷ r

where P is the starting principal, A the yearly addition and n the number of years. The estimated income is the level monthly payment that would draw the balance down to exactly $0 by the end of the payout period, with the remaining money still growing at the payout rate.

Worked example

You start with $25,000, add $5,000 at the end of each year and earn 5% a year for 15 years.

Ending balance$159,866.02
Total additions$75,000.00
Growth earned$59,866.02
Estimated monthly income for 20 years at 4%$962.74

Over 20 years those payments add up to $231,058.36, more than the balance, because the money not yet paid out keeps growing. Moving the additions to the start of each year raises the ending balance to $165,260.66 and the monthly income to $991.98.

What this estimate leaves out

  • Insurer pricing: a lifetime income annuity is priced on life expectancy, so a real quote can differ from a fixed-period estimate.
  • Fees and riders: mortality and expense charges, administrative fees and optional riders reduce the credited rate. Enter the rate after fees for a closer estimate.
  • Surrender charges: many annuities charge a penalty for withdrawals in the early years.
  • Taxes: growth in a deferred annuity is generally taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn, and withdrawals before age 59½ may face an extra 10% federal tax.

faq.question: What is the difference between an annuity due and an ordinary annuity?
faq.answer: In an annuity due, each payment is made at the start of the period; in an ordinary annuity, at the end. Paying in at the start gives each addition one more period of growth, so the ending balance is higher.

faq.question: Is the growth rate guaranteed?
faq.answer: Only if your contract guarantees it. Fixed annuities credit a declared rate, while variable and indexed annuities depend on investment or index performance. For those, treat the rate as an assumption and try a range.

faq.question: Does the estimated income last for life?
faq.answer: No. It is a level payment for the number of years you choose, after which the balance reaches $0. Lifetime payouts from an insurer depend on age, sex and the contract's terms, so ask for a quote to compare.

faq.question: Can I use this for an IRA or 401(k) rather than an annuity?
faq.answer: The arithmetic is the same for any account that grows at a steady rate with regular additions. Contribution limits and tax rules differ, so a dedicated retirement account calculator is more suitable for those plans.

faq.question: Why does the payout total exceed the ending balance?
faq.answer: The part of the balance you have not yet withdrawn keeps earning the payout rate. That growth is added to each payment, so total income over the payout period is larger than the starting balance whenever the payout rate is above 0%.
